items.title: [Bug fix] Fix tilize kernel API misuses causing silent wrong data
items.body:
### Ticket
#51215 

### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Fixes findings 1 and 4 from issue #51215 (findings 2 and 3 — the `sort_single_row_multi_core` path — are tracked separately and not included here).

**Finding 1 — `retile.cpp`: missing pack-format reconfiguration before tilize**
The retile compute kernel entered the tilize phase without calling `pack_reconfig_data_format` to switch the packer's destination format from `mid_cb` (input format) to `out_cb` (output format). When `ttnn.tilize` changes both tile shape and dtype (e.g. `BFLOAT16 → BFLOAT8_B`), every tile packed into `out_cb` was emitted in the input data format, producing a corrupt output tensor. Fix: insert `pack_reconfig_data_format(mid_cb, out_cb)` immediately before `tilize_init`.

**Finding 4 — `reader_unary_pad_dims_split_rows.cpp`: misaligned column-padding stores**
The single-core padding reader cast an arbitrarily-offset L1 address to `uint32_t*` and wrote whole 4-byte words. When the unpadded row size is not a multiple of 4 bytes (e.g. `bfloat16` width=31 → 62 bytes/row), the integer-division loop ran too few iterations (silently dropped the tail bytes) and the misaligned 32-bit stores overwrote the last real input bytes. Fix: replace the naive loop with the alignment-aware `dataflow_kernel_lib::fill_l1_range<elem_size>()` from `kernel_lib/l1_helpers.hpp`, shared by all three padding readers to prevent future divergence.

### Notes for reviewers
- The alignment-aware fill helper lives in `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/kernel_lib/l1_helpers.hpp` as `dataflow_kernel_lib::fill_l1_range<val_size>`. All three `tilize_with_val_padding` readers now use it; the `both_dims` reader keeps its `common.hpp` include only for `tt_memmove`.
- The helper clamps `start_addr_4B`/`end_addr_4B` so that short, unaligned ranges (where the aligned interior is empty) never extend the head/tail element-loops outside `[start_addr, end_addr)`.
- `elem_size` is now passed to the single-core reader as compile-time arg 2; the factory change is in `tilize_with_val_padding_single_core_program_factory.cpp`.
- Regression tests added for both findings; the FP8 test is gated to Blackhole (`@run_for_blackhole()`).

items.title: [Bug fix]: Workaround upper 16 TCs corrupting mirrored TCs by remapping upper TCs to an unused shadow
items.body:
### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Resnet on Quasar debug helped surface a HW issue with the upper 16 tile counters of each Tensix that by default do not get mirrored to the Overlay. 

The bug is that when tile counter A (>= 16) is programmed/used, tile counter A % 16 gets corrupted because TCs >= 16 are represented by 5 bits in remapper but overlay tensix are represented by 4 bits. The workaround is to remap tile counter A to another tile counter B (>= 16) and have both producer and consumer of the intra-tensix DFB use tile counter A. This means we can only have a total of 8 fully parallelized intra-tensix DFBs. 

Why was it not caught earlier?
Our intra-t6 DFB + DM->Tensix/Tensix->DM DFB tests were only testing that the host side config for both were set up correctly and both being able to push/pop credits (and the tests were only pushing/popping one credit at a time). Since the capacities didn't conflict with each other, this issue was never caught. We are planning to add randomized testing.

items.title: ttnn.fmod: returns values outside [0, |s|) and with the wrong sign for |x| >~ 1e7
items.body:
`ttnn.fmod(x, scalar)` does not satisfy the defining contract of `fmod`. For moderately large `|x|` it returns values whose magnitude exceeds the modulus and whose sign is opposite to `x`. This is not an accuracy shortfall — the returned values are outside the set of mathematically possible answers.

`ttnn.remainder` shares the same kernel structure and is affected identically; measurements for it are in the section below.

| x | s | ttnn.fmod | torch.fmod | violation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e8 | 3 | 0 | 1 | wrong value |
| 1e10 | 3 | **-1021** | 1 | `\|result\| >= s`, wrong sign |
| 1e15 | 3 | **-6.71089e+07** | 2 | `\|result\| >= s`, wrong sign |
| -1e10 | 3 | **-1024** | -1 | `\|result\| >= s` |
| 1e8 | 7 | **-1** | 2 | wrong sign |

Measured over uniform samples with `s = 3` (reference is `math.fmod` of the **float32-rounded** operands, so fp32 input quantisation is not counted against the kernel):

| \|x\| range | wrong | `\|result\| >= s` | wrong sign |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1e2 .. 1e4 | 0.00% | 0.00% | 0.00% |
| 1e5 .. 1e6 | 0.50% | 0.00% | 0.00% |
| 1e6 .. 1e7 | 5.38% | 0.00% | 0.00% |
| 1e7 .. 1e8 | 59.85% | 5.65% | 18.10% |
| 1e8 .. 1e9 | 66.42% | 33.62% | 33.62% |
| 1e9 .. 1e11 | 67.50% | 27.70% | 27.70% |

## Root cause

Two independent defects in `calculate_fmod()` (`ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h`; the Blackhole copy differs only in `sfpi::` qualification, so both architectures are affected).

**1. The residue is formed by a subtraction that cannot represent it.** The kernel computes `v - quotient*s` in fp32. Once the fp32 spacing at `v` exceeds `s`, the difference is quantised far more coarsely than the answer:

| \|x\| | fp32 spacing | answer must be |
|---|---|---|
| 1e7 | 1 | < 3 |
| 1e8 | 8 | < 3 |
| 1e10 | 1024 | < 3 |
| 1e12 | 6.55e4 | < 3 |

At `|x| = 1e10` the spacing is 1024 — which is exactly the scale of the observed `-1021` result.

**2. The repair loop negates instead of reducing.** The trailing loop is

```cpp
for (int l = 0; l < iter; l++) {
    v_if(v >= s) { v = s - v; }   // negates
    v_endif;
}
```

For `v >= s` this yields a negative number rather than reducing `v` modulo `s`, and the loop then exits because the negative value is no longer `>= s`. The sign is already fixed by `copysgn` before this point, so the negation survives into the output. Concretely, at `x = 33554740`, `s = 3`:

| | value |
|---|---|
| before the loop | 4 |
| as shipped (`v = s - v`) | **-1** |
| with `v = v - s` | **1** |
| `torch.fmod` | **1** |

The corrected direction lands exactly on the right answer here.

## ttnn.remainder is affected the same way

`calculate_remainder()` in `ckernel_sfpu_remainder.h` reuses the same quotient / subtract / repair-loop structure, including the identical `v = s - v` loop. Porting it the same way and comparing against `torch.remainder` semantics (result takes the sign of the divisor, so `0 <= result < s` for `s > 0`):

| x | s | ttnn.remainder | torch.remainder |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1e10 | 3 | **-1021** | 1 |
| 1e15 | 3 | **-6.71089e+07** | 2 |
| -1e10 | 3 | **-1024** | 2 |
| 1e9 | 7 | **-57** | 6 |

| \|x\| range (s=3) | wrong | outside `[0, s)` |
|---|---|---|
| 1e2 .. 1e4 | 0.00% | 0.00% |
| 1e6 .. 1e7 | 5.43% | 0.00% |
| 1e7 .. 1e8 | 60.43% | 18.23% |
| 1e8 .. 1e9 | 65.73% | 32.00% |
| 1e9 .. 1e11 | 67.50% | 28.13% |

Same onset, same magnitudes. I've kept this in one issue since it is one root cause in two copies; happy to split it if you'd rather track them separately.

## Why it shipped

`test_div_ops.py::test_fmod_scalar` draws its inputs from `torch_random(low=-100, high=100)`. Measured failure rate for `|x| <= 100` is **0.00%** — the test samples only the region that works. The failure begins around `|x| ~ 1e6` and dominates above `1e7`. The remainder tests cover the same narrow band.

## Proposed fix

Two changes, of different scope:

- **Loop direction** (one line, both kernels): `v = s - v` → `v = v - s`. Measured on `s = 7`, this drops `|result| >= s` from 52.77% to 0.53% over `[1e8, 1e9]`, and does not regress `|x| <= 100` (0 / 20000 wrong).
- **Argument reduction** (the real fix): the loop-direction change does not help above `~1e9`, where the residue is simply not representable by `v - quotient*s`. A correct `fmod` needs genuine range reduction — e.g. repeated reduction by `s * 2^k` from the top, which keeps every intermediate exactly representable.

I'd treat these as separate changes; the first is a strict improvement and easy to review on its own.

## Suggested checklist

- [ ] Fix the repair-loop direction in `ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h` and `ckernel_sfpu_remainder.h` (Wormhole + Blackhole)
- [ ] Implement argument reduction so `|x| > s * 2^23` is handled exactly
- [ ] Extend `test_fmod_scalar` and the remainder tests beyond `[-100, 100]`
- [ ] Add invariant assertions to both: `|result| < |s|`, and the correct sign convention for each op

A reproduction script (a float32 port of `calculate_fmod`, so no Tenstorrent hardware is required) is in the first comment below.

---

*Disclosure: this analysis and the reproduction script were produced by an AI agent working on my behalf. I'm posting it and will route any questions, but I won't claim personal authorship of the derivations. Nothing here rests on taking my word for it: the script below reproduces every number in this report in a few seconds on CPU, with no Tenstorrent hardware, so the claims are independently checkable.*

items.title: Fix ttnn.sort wrong indices for bf16
items.body:
### PR Category

Bug fix

### Summary

Fixes #46331 — `ttnn.sort` returns wrong indices for integer keys larger than ~256.

**Root cause.** The sort's TopK SFPU LLK (`ckernel::topk_local_sort`) compares tile values in **bf16** by default. bf16 has only an 8-bit mantissa, so integers above 256 (e.g. `257`, `258`, `259`) all round to the same bf16 value and become equal to the comparator. The comparator then leaves the two tied elements in whatever order the merge-sort network happened to place them, so the returned indices are non-deterministic and can be wrong for any input with:
* dtype `UINT16` or `FLOAT32` outside the exact-bf16 range, or
* dtype `BFLOAT16` where the user's numeric range collides after truncation.

Prior workaround (`createSortOpOperandsWorkarounds`, casting integer input → `ui16` on host) only kept the op runnable; the comparison precision was still bf16, so the **indices** stayed wrong.

**Fix.** Sort keys are now compared as `Float32` on the SFPU:
* `FLOAT32` input: unchanged path — already ran the sort kernel with `fp32_dest_acc_en = true`.
* `UINT16` input: promoted to `Float32` for the sort:
  * The reader kernel DMAs raw `UInt16` tiles into a staging CB (`c_11` / `c_12`) and software-converts each element to `Float32` on the Baby RISC-V core into a `Float32` primary CB (`c_0`). All values in `[0, 65535]` are exactly representable in Float32's 24-bit mantissa, so the comparison is exact. Hardware unpack cannot numerically convert `UInt16 → Float32` per the Tensix ISA (only `UInt16 → UInt16` dest is supported), which is why the cast is done on the RISC-V core with an explicit `__sync_synchronize()` fence before `push_back` so the compute kernel sees the completed stores.
  * The writer kernel does the reverse: it software-converts the sorted `Float32` values back to `UInt16` in a staging CB, then DMAs the result to DRAM.
  * Because `fp32_dest_acc_en = true` forces the sort kernel to use `INT32` (4 KB) index tiles, `UINT16` inputs now return **`UINT32`** indices (matching what `FLOAT32` inputs already did).
* `BFLOAT16` input: no behavioral change (already the bf16-comparison path; users needing exact-int index guarantees should pass `UINT16` or `FLOAT32`).

**Additional coverage added along the way** while wiring the `Float32` conversion through all three program factories:
* `SortProgramFactorySingleRowSingleCore` — reader/writer conversion + fence for both TILE and ROW_MAJOR layouts.
* `SortProgramFactorySingleRowMultiCore` — reader/writer conversion for both TILE and ROW_MAJOR layouts, plus a fix for a latent DMA sizing bug in the coordinator's passthrough (used `get_tile_size(c_0)` which is now `Float32` = 4 KB when the DRAM tiles are `UInt16` = 2 KB).
* MultiCore ROW_MAJOR path was rewritten to use a pair-row CB layout (each `c_6` / `c_8` page holds one row of both tiles side-by-side) so `tilize_block(cb, 2)` produces the expected 2-tile output. This fixes a pre-existing layout bug in the MultiCore RM path.
* `SortDeviceOperation::select_program_factory` — `UINT16` inputs above the SingleCore threshold now route to `SortProgramFactorySingleRowMultiCore` (the CrossCore factory does not yet implement the `UInt16 ↔ Float32` conversion CBs).
* `UINT16` + ROW_MAJOR uses a lower SingleCore threshold (`Wt <= 32`), because promoting the SingleCore RM value CBs to `Float32` doubles per-row storage and `Wt = 64` would OOM ~2 MB in a 1.5 MB L1. Larger `Wt` routes to MultiCore, which uses per-tile pages independent of `Wt`.

### Notes for reviewers

* The comparison-precision fix is entirely on-device — no host-side typecast, no change to the public API surface other than the `UINT16 → UINT32` index dtype (which matches the pre-existing `FLOAT32` input contract).
* `UINT16` padding uses `UINT16_MAX` (ascending) / `0` (descending) as sentinels because `UInt16` cannot represent `±inf`. This has a **known limitation** when the input contains those exact values AND the last dim needs W-padding to the next power of two: since the sort is unstable, a padded element can tie with the real value at the slice boundary and yield an index outside the original last dim. Follow-up work is to have the reader kernel override the padded region with a `Float32` sentinel keyed off `original_last_dim`.
* Files most worth focusing on:
  * `sort_program_factory.cpp` — CB format promotion, `fp32_dest_acc_en`, `UnpackToDestFp32`, new staging CBs.
  * `reader_single_row_{single,multi}_core.cpp`, `writer_single_row_{single,multi}_core.cpp` — RISC-V `UInt16 ↔ Float32` conversion loops with `__sync_synchronize()` fences.
  * `sort_device_operation.cpp` — routing threshold changes for `UINT16` inputs.
  * `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/data_movement/test_sort.py` — regression coverage: `test_sort_uint16_index_correctness`, `test_sort_uint16_row_major_correctness`, `test_sort_uint16_index_correctness_multicore` covering the ranges that used to alias in bf16.
* Full `test_sort.py` suite: **125 passed** locally on WH.

items.title: [Bug] bfloat16 loses all 254 NaN encodings through ops that neither convert nor compute
items.body:
## Describe the bug

A `bfloat16` NaN does not survive a device op, even an op that performs no arithmetic and no format conversion. `ttnn.to_layout`, `ttnn.neg`, `ttnn.abs` and `ttnn.typecast(x, ttnn.bfloat16)` all return an Infinity of the same sign. A host round-trip and `ttnn.clone` preserve the value, so it reaches the device intact and is destroyed on the way back out.

In-tree this is recorded in 15 places as an expected hardware limitation of the dtype, for example `ternary_program_factory.cpp:939`: *"bfloat16 packs NaN as inf as this is an expected behaviour and a known HW limitation of bfloat16 dtype."* That is not what I measure. I have a build in which **all 254 bfloat16 NaN encodings survive these ops bit-exact**, with **all 65024 normal encodings unchanged** and no perf change I can detect. See the note at the end.

## Relationship to the two open issues this subsumes

Both of these are the same defect seen through one op each. I am filing this rather than commenting on either, because the behaviour is not specific to the op in either title, and because the fix makes both of their repros pass.

- #31406, open since 2025-10-29. Its exact repro, all four layout combinations, both dtypes, on Blackhole P300:

  | dtype | direction | unpatched | with my fix |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | float32 | all four combinations | NaN kept | NaN kept |
  | bfloat16 | ROW_MAJOR -> ROW_MAJOR | NaN kept (no conversion happens) | NaN kept |
  | bfloat16 | ROW_MAJOR -> TILE | **`+Inf`** | **NaN kept** |
  | bfloat16 | TILE -> ROW_MAJOR | **`+Inf`** | **NaN kept** |
  | bfloat16 | TILE -> TILE | NaN kept (no conversion happens) | NaN kept |

  Two notes on that issue. Its float32 claim, NaN becoming `131008.0`, no longer reproduces on Blackhole at `66d22c1f3a9`: float32 NaN survives all four combinations, so what remains of #31406 is the bfloat16 case. And #19585, which #31406 was split out of, is closed.
- #40503, open since 2026-03-23. Measured below.

What is new here relative to both: it is not one op, it is every op in the class, including `neg`, `abs` and `typecast(x, bfloat16)`; it is exhaustive over all 65536 bfloat16 encodings rather than one NaN; and the fix exists and is measured.

## To reproduce

```python
import torch, ttnn

d = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)

def bf16(bits):                      # a 32x32 bfloat16 tile whose first element is `bits`
    r = torch.zeros(1, 1, 32, 32, dtype=torch.int16)
    r[0, 0, 0, 0] = bits - (1 << 16) if bits >= 0x8000 else bits
    return ttnn.from_torch(r.view(torch.bfloat16), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
                           layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=d)

def bits(t):
    return int(ttnn.to_torch(t).view(torch.int16).flatten()[0].item()) & 0xFFFF

print(f"round-trip, no op  0x{bits(bf16(0x7FC0)):04X}")                                             # 7FC0
print(f"clone              0x{bits(ttnn.clone(bf16(0x7FC0), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16)):04X}")            # 7FC0
print(f"to_layout ROW_MAJOR 0x{bits(ttnn.to_layout(bf16(0x7FC0), ttnn.ROW_MAJOR_LAYOUT)):04X}")     # 7F80  <-- +Inf
print(f"neg                0x{bits(ttnn.neg(bf16(0x7FC0))):04X}")                                   # FF80  <-- -Inf
print(f"abs                0x{bits(ttnn.abs(bf16(0x7FC0))):04X}")                                   # 7F80  <-- +Inf
print(f"typecast bf16->bf16 0x{bits(ttnn.typecast(bf16(0x7FC0), ttnn.bfloat16)):04X}")               # 7F80  <-- +Inf
```

Measured on Blackhole P300. `0x7FC0` is a quiet NaN; `0x7F80` is `+Inf`. The same holds for every other NaN encoding, e.g. `0x7F81 -> 0x7F80` and `0xFFC0 -> 0xFF80`.

Build a fresh input for each measurement and read each result once: several ttnn ops deallocate their input, so reusing one device tensor across ops reads a freed buffer.

## Exhaustive measurement

All 65536 bfloat16 bit patterns in a single `[1, 1, 256, 256]` tensor, one op applied to one freshly built tensor, on Blackhole P300:

| op | words changed of 65536 | NaN encodings changed | normal encodings changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| host round-trip, no device op | 0 | 0 of 254 | 0 of 65024 |
| `clone` bf16 -> bf16 | 0 | 0 of 254 | 0 of 65024 |
| `to_layout` TILE -> ROW_MAJOR | 509 | **254 of 254**, to `0x7F80` / `0xFF80` | 0 of 65024 |
| `neg` | 65535 (a sign flip changes almost everything, as expected) | **254 of 254**, to `0xFF80` / `0x7F80` | — |

`to_layout` broken down by class, on the unpatched build and on the build with my fix:

| class | count | unpatched | with my fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| normal | 65024 | 0 changed | 0 changed |
| **NaN** | 254 | **all 254 -> ±Inf**, 2 distinct outputs | **0 changed**, 254 distinct outputs, bit-exact |
| denormal | 254 | all -> `0x0000` | all -> `0x0000`, unchanged |
| −0 | 1 | -> `+0` | -> `+0`, unchanged |
| Inf | 2 | 0 changed | 0 changed |

Every normal value is bit-exact in both builds, which is the evidence that preserving the NaN does not disturb ordinary data. `ttnn.neg` likewise returns 254 distinct NaNs with my fix (`0xFF81`, `0xFF82`, ...), i.e. sign flipped and payload preserved, which is correct IEEE negation of a NaN.

## #40503 measured

#40503 carries an AI-generated root-cause guess that points at the SFPU write. That guess is wrong: the value the SFPU writes is fine, and it is lost afterwards, which is why `clone` and the host round-trip keep it while `full_like` does not. Measured with the same helpers as above:

```
ttnn.full_like(bf16 tensor, float("nan"))   unpatched 0x7F80        with my fix 0x7FC0
```

So one change closes both #40503 and the bfloat16 half of #31406, which is all that is left of it.

## In-tree workarounds this explains

15 places in 8 files work around the behaviour, all describing it as expected and none of them correct about why. `test_exp2.py:222-225` is worth singling out: it states that *"ttnn.bfloat16 host-side packing collapses NaN to +inf before the tensor reaches the SFPU"*, and the round-trip line in the repro above shows that is not so — the host path carries all 254 encodings intact.

- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_unary.py:461`, `:2546`, `:2658`, `:2662`
- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_where.py:407`, `:435`, `:472`
- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_div_ops.py:407`, `:445`
- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_pow.py:167`
- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_expm1.py:42`
- `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_exp2.py:222-225`
- `tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_unary_shard.py:208`, `:218`
- `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/ternary/device/ternary_program_factory.cpp:939`, which describes a
  workaround of reinterpreting the bfloat16 CBs as `UINT16` so the datapath bit-copies instead of
  converting

## Expected behavior

`torch` preserves a NaN through negation and through `float32 -> bfloat16` (`0x7FC00000 -> 0x7FC0`). Independently of torch parity, a NaN silently becoming `+Inf` is worse than an abort: NaN is what a user greps for when debugging, `Inf` compares and propagates differently, and a NaN guard placed after any bfloat16 op will never fire. `bfloat16` represents NaN perfectly well, so describing this as a limitation of the dtype is inaccurate.

## Scope of this report

- Only ops that **neither convert a format nor perform arithmetic** are in scope. A genuine narrowing conversion such as `typecast(float32, bfloat16)` still yields `+Inf` from a NaN and is **not** claimed here.
- **Denormals are not part of this report.** All 254 still become `+0`, and `tech_reports/Handling_Special_Value/special_values.md` documents denormals as flushed globally in TT hardware (`denormals | all | 0x0`), so that is intended.
- **Minus zero is not part of this report.** It still becomes `+0`. One word out of 65536, and I have not isolated where it is lost, so I make no claim about it.
- Measured on **Blackhole** only. I have no Wormhole hardware.

## Environment

- Blackhole P300, device 0
- tt-metal `66d22c1f3a9`; the LLK sources involved are byte-identical to `main` at `b6d87f377ba`
- sfpi 7.67.0

## Note on the fix

I have root-caused this and I have a fix. It is small, it is confined to the LLK, and it is measured on Blackhole P300:

- all 254 NaN encodings preserved bit-exact through the ops above, with sign and payload;
- all 65024 normal encodings bit-identical to the unpatched build;
- #40503 fixed (`full_like(nan)` returns `0x7FC0`) and #31406's repro passing in all eight dtype-by-direction combinations;
- ttnn eltwise regression subset: **1064 passed, 455 skipped, 0 failed**;
- no perf change I can detect: an LLK unary SFPU sweep restricted to `Float16_b`, before and after, moves by well under 1% in both directions, i.e. noise.

I have not opened a PR yet because I would rather confirm the diagnosis with you first and avoid duplicating work someone else may already have in flight. If you would like the change, please assign the issue to me and I will submit it.

items.title: [tt_metal/hw][SFPU] isclose compares Inf/NaN bit pattern as a float magnitude (WH + BH)
items.body:
Sub-issue of #51220, covering **items 1 and 2** (the same defect in the Wormhole and Blackhole copies of `ckernel_sfpu_isclose.h`).

### Defect

The Inf/NaN fix-up in `calculate_sfpu_isclose` compares **float magnitudes** against `inf_bits`, which is declared as an integer bit pattern:

```cpp
constexpr int32_t inf_bits = 0x7F800000;   // documented as "IEEE-754 abs(+inf)"
...
sfpi::vFloat a_abs = sfpi::abs(a);
v_if(a_abs >= inf_bits || b_abs >= inf_bits) {   // float compare, not bit compare
```

sfpi declares `operator>=(vFloat, vFloat)` and `operator>=(vFloat, float)` (`sfpi.h:490/498`) but no `(vFloat, int32_t)`, and `vFloat` has no conversion to `vInt`. The only viable overload is the float one, so `0x7F800000` is converted to the finite value `2139095040.0f` and the intended exponent test (`exp == 0xFF`) silently becomes a magnitude test.

### Impact — silently wrong results on WH and BH

| Input | `torch.isclose` | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `isclose(+inf, +inf)` | True | **False** |
| `isclose(-inf, -inf)` | True | **False** |
| `isclose(3e9, 3e9)` | True | **False** |
| `isclose(1e10, 1e10)` | True | **False** |
| `isclose(-NaN, -NaN)`, `equal_nan=True` | True | **False** |

Any two bit-identical finite operands with `|x| > 2139095040.0f` compare as *not close*. Confirmed on n150 (WormholeB0); the boundary sits at exactly `float(0x7F800000)` to the ulp (`2139094912.0` → True, `2139095168.0` → False).

`-NaN` is a second, independent facet found while fixing this: it was untested and also broken.

### Why it was not caught

`tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_relational.py::test_isclose_inf_divergence` only exercised *mismatched* infinities (expected `False`), which the broken code happens to produce. Every other isclose test stays within ±150, and no test used `-NaN`.

### Fix

Mask the integer views to abs bit patterns and compare those, so the predicates bind to `operator>=/>/==(vInt, int32_t)`. The mask is held in `vConstIntPrgm0` (programmed by a new `isclose_init`) to keep it out of the replay block.

Note for future readers: the mask **cannot** be replaced by bit-casting `sfpi::abs()`. Per the [`SFPABS` functional model](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-isa-documentation/blob/main/WormholeB0/TensixTile/TensixCoprocessor/SFPABS.md) (shared verbatim by WH and BH), float mode deliberately leaves `-NaN` as `-NaN` rather than clearing the sign bit, so a bit-cast `abs()` yields a negative int32 for `-NaN` and skips the fix-up entirely.

### Verification

n150 (WormholeB0): the new regression tests fail 17 without the kernel change and pass with it; full `test_relational.py` 218/218. Blackhole is code-identical but has not been run on BH silicon locally — CI's `llk_smoke_blackhole` covers that.

Item 3 of #51220 (Quasar `exp` range guards) is a separate defect and is not in scope here.

items.title: [SFPU] isclose: compare Inf/NaN bit patterns as vInt, not float magnitudes
items.body:
### Problem

`isclose`'s Inf/NaN fix-up compared **float magnitudes** against `inf_bits`, which is declared as an integer bit pattern:

```cpp
constexpr int32_t inf_bits = 0x7F800000;   // documented as "IEEE-754 abs(+inf)"
...
sfpi::vFloat a_abs = sfpi::abs(a);
v_if(a_abs >= inf_bits || b_abs >= inf_bits) {   // <-- float compare, not bit compare
```

sfpi declares `operator>=(vFloat, vFloat)` and `operator>=(vFloat, float)` (`sfpi.h:490/498`) but **no** `(vFloat, int32_t)`, and `vFloat` has no conversion to `vInt`. The only viable overload is the float one, so `0x7F800000` was converted to the finite value `2139095040.0f`. The intended exponent test (`exp == 0xFF`) silently became a plain magnitude test.

Wrong results on both Wormhole and Blackhole:

| Input | `torch.isclose` | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `isclose(+inf, +inf)` | True | **False** | True |
| `isclose(-inf, -inf)` | True | **False** | True |
| `isclose(3e9, 3e9)` | True | **False** | True |
| `isclose(1e10, 1e10)` | True | **False** | True |
| `isclose(-NaN, -NaN)`, `equal_nan=True` | True | **False** | True |
| `isclose(+inf, -inf)` | False | False | False |

The finite-value failures are the wider blast radius: any two bit-identical operands with `|x| > 2139095040.0f` compared as *not close*.

### Fix

Mask the already-computed integer views to abs bit patterns and compare those, so the three special-case predicates bind to `operator>=/>/==(vInt, int32_t)` (`sfpi.h:517/520/522`):

```cpp
sfpi::vInt a_abs_bits = a_bits & sfpi::vConstIntPrgm0;   // 0x7FFFFFFF
sfpi::vInt b_abs_bits = b_bits & sfpi::vConstIntPrgm0;
```

The mask lives in a programmable constant register, programmed once by a new `isclose_init` wired through `SFPU_BINARY_INIT_FN_NO_ARGS`, following the `ckernel_sfpu_sqrt.h:120` / `recip_init` precedent. An inline `& 0x7FFFFFFF` would rebuild the mask with a per-element `SFPLOADI` inside the replay block — the cost `ckernel_sfpu_abs.h:30-32` records as +30% cyc/tile for that kernel. Static SFPU instruction count in `calculate_sfpu_isclose`, measured by compiling the real math TU with the JIT's own command:

| | pre-fix | inline mask | bit-cast `abs()` | **const reg (this PR)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SFPLOADI | 6 | 32 | 12 | 12 |
| TOTAL | 120 | 139 | 83 | **107** |

This is safe because the three `BINARY_SFPU_INIT` guards in the binary_ng compute kernels are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, LHS/RHS activations run in `PREPROCESS` *before* the init, POST activations force a per-tile re-init, and `invoke_binary_ng_isclose` passes no activations at all today.

**The mask cannot be replaced by bit-casting `sfpi::abs()`.** Per the [`SFPABS` functional model](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-isa-documentation/blob/main/WormholeB0/TensixTile/TensixCoprocessor/SFPABS.md) (shared verbatim by Wormhole and Blackhole), float mode deliberately leaves `-NaN` as `-NaN` instead of clearing the sign bit:

```c
if (Mod1 & SFPABS_MOD1_FLOAT) {
  if (x > 0xff800000u) { /* Value is -NaN; leave it as -NaN. */ }
  else { x &= 0x7fffffffu; }
}
```

A bit-cast `abs()` therefore yields a negative int32 for `-NaN`, `a_abs_bits >= inf_bits` is false, and the fix-up is skipped — measured on n150 as `isclose(-NaN, 1.0) == True` with `equal_nan=False`. The kernel comment records this so it does not get "optimized" into the broken form. `b_abs` stays a `vFloat`; it is still needed for the `atol + rtol * |b|` term.

The sibling kernel `ckernel_sfpu_log1p.h:123` uses the same bit-compare idiom and notes it can skip masking only *"since u>=0"*; `isclose` operands can be negative, hence the explicit sign-bit clear.

Applies to the Wormhole and Blackhole copies, which were and remain byte-identical. **Quasar is not affected** — it has no `ckernel_sfpu_isclose.h`, so there is nothing to port.

### Tests

`test_isclose_inf_divergence` only checked *mismatched* infinities (expected `False`), which the broken kernel happened to produce, and every other isclose test stayed within ±150. It is replaced with:

- `test_isclose_special_values` — full cross product of signed zeros, ±Inf, ±NaN and large finite magnitudes, over fp32/bf16 × `equal_nan` ∈ {True, False}. Subsumes the old divergent-Inf case and adds matching Inf.
- `test_isclose_matching_infinities` — `isclose(±inf, ±inf)` True, mismatched signs False.
- `test_isclose_large_finite_magnitudes` — equal finite operands across `2e9 … FLT_MAX`, both signs.
- `test_isclose_negative_nan` — bit-exact `0xFFC00000`, both `equal_nan` modes. `-NaN` was untested and already broken before this branch.
- `test_isclose_inf_bit_pattern_boundary` — bit-exact ulp sweep straddling `float(0x7F800000)` with `rtol=atol=0`, the tightest anchor for this defect.

Failures now carry the offending `a`/`b` values instead of a bare `torch.equal` assert.

### Verification (n150, WormholeB0)

- Without the kernel change: **17 failed / 49 passed** — the new tests genuinely fail without the fix.
- With it: all isclose tests pass; full `test_relational.py` **218/218**.
- Also green: `test_binary_dtype_validation.py -k isclose`, `docs_examples/test_pointwise_binary_examples.py -k isclose`.
- Boundary confirmed empirically at exactly `2139095040.0` before the fix (`2139094912.0` → True, `2139095168.0` → False), matching `float(0x7F800000)` to the ulp.
- Op-level throughput unchanged: `isclose` is DRAM-bandwidth bound (fp32 0.2614ms vs `add` 0.2582ms / `eq` 0.2575ms over 4096 tiles at ~185 GB/s; bf16 1.9× faster, tracking bytes). All variants land within noise.

Blackhole is code-identical to the verified Wormhole path but has not been run on BH silicon.

Fixes #51540 — sub-issue of #51220, covering items 1 and 2. Item 3 of #51220 (Quasar `exp` range guards) is a separate defect and is not touched here.

items.title: DRAM ND-sharded buffer corrupts data when shard grid has duplicate x-coords
items.body:
### Description

For a DRAM buffer, the bank id is the core's **x** coordinate alone. `TensorAccessor::get_noc_addr` calls `get_dram_bank_base_offset(bank_x)` and ignores `bank_y` (`tt_metal/hw/inc/api/tensor/tensor_accessor.h`), and the host agrees — it deliberately does not virtualize DRAM coords "since we need logical x coord == bank_id" (`tt_metal/impl/buffers/tensor_accessor_args.cpp`).

So a shard grid like `CoreRange((0,0), (1,1))` has 4 cores but only 2 distinct x values. Cores `(0,0)`/`(0,1)` both map to bank 0 and `(1,0)`/`(1,1)` both map to bank 1. Two different shards get written to the same place, and one overwrites the other.

Nothing rejects this. The buffer allocates, the write succeeds, and the data is wrong.

### Steps to reproduce

Repro pytest:
```python
import torch, ttnn, pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize("grid_end", [(3, 0), (1, 1)], ids=["one_row_ok", "two_rows_aliases"])
def test_dram_nd_shard_bank_aliasing(device, grid_end):
    grid = ttnn.CoreRangeSet([ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(0, 0), ttnn.CoreCoord(*grid_end))])
    mem_config = ttnn.MemoryConfig(
        ttnn.BufferType.DRAM, ttnn.NdShardSpec(ttnn.Shape([1, 1, 32, 64]), grid)
    )

    torch_input = torch.arange(0, 2 * 3 * 64 * 128, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(2, 3, 64, 128)
    torch_input = torch_input.to(torch.bfloat16)

    tt = ttnn.from_torch(
        torch_input,
        dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
        layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT,
        device=device,
        memory_config=mem_config,
    )
    assert torch.equal(ttnn.to_torch(tt), torch_input)
```

items.title: ttnn.maximum / ttnn.minimum / ttnn.clamp / ttnn.hardtanh silently drop NaN — a single SFPSWAP is a permutation, so max and min can never both return NaN
items.body:
# ttnn.maximum / ttnn.minimum / ttnn.clamp / ttnn.hardtanh silently drop NaN — a single SFPSWAP is a permutation, so max and min can never both return NaN

`ttnn.maximum`, `ttnn.minimum`, `ttnn.clamp` and `ttnn.hardtanh` are each implemented by one or two bare `SFPSWAP` instructions. `SFPSWAP` is a compare-and-exchange, so its two output registers always hold a **permutation** of its two inputs. PyTorch requires `torch.maximum(NaN, x)` **and** `torch.minimum(NaN, x)` to *both* return NaN — a permutation of `{NaN, x}` can never be `(NaN, NaN)`.

This is a purely structural argument: **at least one of `ttnn.maximum` / `ttnn.minimum` is wrong for every NaN input, on both Wormhole and Blackhole, regardless of how the hardware orders NaN.**

Concretely, NaN is silently replaced by the other operand:

* `ttnn.minimum(NaN, 5.0)` returns `5.0`
* `ttnn.maximum(-NaN, 5.0)` returns `5.0`
* `ttnn.clamp(NaN, -2.0, 2.0)` returns `2.0`

The int32 variant in the same kernel already applies a correction for `SFPSWAP` ordering, so there is a ready structural precedent for what the float32 path would need.

### Summary

`SFPSWAP` is the hardware compare-and-exchange used for min/max. Three in-repo facts establish that it is a permutation:

1. `sfpi_lib.h:428` `min_max()` issues a single `__builtin_rvtt_sfpswap` and then uses `sfpselect2` to pick one of *that one instruction's* two outputs.
2. `swap(a, b)` in the same header is `SFPSWAP_MOD1_SWAP` — the instruction's semantics are literally "exchange or don't".
3. `ckernel_sfpu_binary_max_min.h:78` contains the comment *"Conditionally swap again to fix the cases where SFPSWAP got the result backwards"* — only a swap network makes "got it backwards, swap again" meaningful.

`calculate_binary_max_min` issues one `TTI_SFPSWAP(0, LREG1, LREG0, SFPSWAP_MOD1_VEC_MIN_MAX)` and then stores `LREG1` for max or `LREG0` for min. The `SFPLOADMACRO` path routes through `binary_max_min_init`'s `InstructionTemplate[0]`, which is the same single `SFPSWAP` (`mod1 = 9` for max, `1` for min). Either way, the two candidate results are a permutation of the two inputs.

Since `torch.maximum` and `torch.minimum` must *both* yield NaN when either operand is NaN, and a permutation of `{NaN, x}` contains exactly one NaN, **one of the two ops is necessarily wrong on every NaN input.** No assumption about the hardware's NaN ordering is needed to reach that conclusion.

Which one is wrong follows from the ordering `SFPSWAP` actually uses. Three in-repo comments state it is sign-magnitude:

* `ckernel_sfpu_unary_max_min.h:80`: *"it expects sign-magnitude integers"*
* `ckernel_sfpu_relu.h:24`: *"the hardware sign-magnitude min/max (SFPSWAP)"*, and `:85`: *"0x80000000 is -0"*

(Both of those comments sit in int32 code paths, but `SFPSWAP`'s comparison
semantics are a property of the instruction, not of the caller — and for IEEE
float32 the sign-magnitude order coincides with the real order on all finite
values and ±inf, which is precisely why the instruction is usable for float
min/max at all. Note also that **the permutation argument above does not depend
on this at all** — the ordering only determines *which* of `maximum`/`minimum`
is wrong for a given NaN sign, not *that* one of them must be.)

For IEEE float32, sign-magnitude integer order agrees with real order on all finite values and ±inf. Extending it to NaN puts `|NaN|` (`0x7FC00000`) above `|inf|` (`0x7F800000`), so `+NaN` sorts highest and `-NaN` sorts lowest. Hence `minimum(+NaN, x) = x` and `maximum(-NaN, x) = x`.

- Files:
  - `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_max_min.h` (WH)
  - `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/blackhole/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_max_min.h` (BH, logic-identical)
  - `ckernel_sfpu_unary_max_min.h`, `ckernel_sfpu_clamp.h`, `ckernel_sfpu_hardtanh.h` (both platforms)
- Fix template, already in-repo: `ckernel_sfpu_comp.h` — see below.

### Measured behaviour

Simulated per-instruction in float32 against `torch` / `numpy` reference. Errors are semantic (a non-NaN value escapes where NaN is required), so relative error is undefined rather than large.

| input | returned | expected |
|---|---|---|
| `ttnn.minimum(+NaN 0x7fc00000, 5.0)` | `5.0` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.minimum(+NaN, -inf)` | `-inf` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.minimum(+NaN, 0.0)` | `0.0` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.maximum(-NaN 0xffc00000, 5.0)` | `5.0` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.maximum(-NaN, +inf)` | `inf` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.clamp(+NaN, min=-2.0, max=2.0)` | `2.0` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.clamp(+NaN, min=0.0, max=6.0)` | `6.0` | `nan (0x7fc00000)` |
| `ttnn.clamp(-NaN, min=0.0, max=6.0)` | `0.0` | `nan (0xffc00000)` |
| `ttnn.hardtanh(+NaN, min_val=-1.0, max_val=1.0)` | `1.0` | `nan` |

As a control, 200,100 random and special **non-NaN** pairs (including ±inf, ±0, subnormals) were run through the same model: **0 mismatches** for both `maximum` and `minimum`. The defect is strictly NaN-specific — this is a semantics bug, not an accuracy claim, so there is no tolerance threshold to argue about.

One detail worth noting for whoever writes the fix: the expected bit patterns above were measured against torch directly, and the two operator families do not agree on the NaN sign. `torch.maximum` / `torch.minimum` normalise the result to `0x7fc00000` regardless of which operand was NaN or what its sign was, whereas `torch.clamp` and `torch.nn.functional.hardtanh` preserve the input's sign bit (`-NaN` in, `0xffc00000` out). A fix for `max`/`min` is therefore free to emit any quiet NaN, but a fix for `clamp`/`hardtanh` should pass the input through rather than substitute a canonical NaN.

### clamp and hardtanh: same root cause, second operator family

`calculate_clamp` is `max` then `min`:

```
load_value_param_float(min_val);  calculate_unary_max_min_float_body<Max>();
load_value_param_float(max_val);  calculate_unary_max_min_float_body<Min>();
```

and each body is a single `TTI_SFPSWAP(0, LREG12, LREG0, ...)`. `hardtanh` calls `sfpi::clamp`, which is `min(max(val, lower), upper)` — the same two swaps.

For NaN to survive, it would have to compare **greater** than `lo` in step one (so `max` keeps it) and **less** than `hi` in step two (so `min` keeps it). A comparator producing a consistent total order cannot do both, so under *any* total ordering of NaN — highest, lowest, or anywhere in between — clamp loses it. Under sign-magnitude order specifically, `+NaN → hi` and `-NaN → lo`.

One further possibility deserves stating explicitly, since ruling it out is what makes the above exhaustive: a comparator could treat NaN as **unordered** and therefore never swap at all. NaN would then survive both steps and `clamp` would be correct. That case is excluded by the same in-tree evidence cited earlier — `SFPSWAP` compares its operands as sign-magnitude **integers**, and integer comparison has no unordered case; every bit pattern has a definite position. If that reading turned out to be wrong, this clamp/hardtanh section would weaken accordingly. **The `maximum`/`minimum` argument would not**: two output slots holding a permutation of two inputs contain exactly one NaN no matter what the comparator decides, ordered or unordered.

### Test gap

`ttnn.maximum` and `ttnn.minimum` do have dedicated coverage — `test_binary_maximum.py` and `test_unary_maximum.py`, plus four sweeps under `sweeps/eltwise/composite/binary/maximum/`. Those tests exercise float32, and they explicitly parametrise special values: `±inf`, `±FLT_MAX`, and the int32 extremes appear across roughly ten cases between the two files.

**Not one of them uses NaN.** Special-value coverage was clearly considered and deliberately built out; NaN is the one class of special value missing from it.

The same gap shows against a standard the repository already applies elsewhere: `test_binary_comp_fp32.py` defines a `_SPECIAL_FP32_GRID` that *does* contain `nan` alongside `±inf`, and uses it to test the tensor–tensor paths of `ttnn.eq/ne/gt/lt/ge/le`.

**The standard already exists** — order-relation operators are expected to be NaN-correct, and there is a special-value grid built to enforce it. `max`/`min` are order relations by the same definition but are not currently covered by that grid, so extending it is a natural fit.

For clamp, `test_backward_clamp.py` is backward-only, all bfloat16, with inputs from `data_gen_with_range(shape, -100, 100)` (finite only) and a min/max parameter list containing no inf and no NaN. There is no forward clamp test file. `test_hardtanh.py` uses `torch.randn(...).bfloat16() * 10` — no NaN, no inf.

### Proposed fix

Detect NaN operands and force a NaN result, before or after the swap. `ckernel_sfpu_comp.h` already contains the idiom this needs — its comment at `:74` reads *"rejects NaN with a single SFPIADD"*, implemented at `:113` as:

```cpp
TTI_SFPIADD(0, INF, ABS_V, sfpi::SFPIADD_MOD1_ARG_2SCOMP_LREG_DST | sfpi::SFPIADD_MOD1_CC_GTE0);
```

i.e. compare `|v|` against the inf bit pattern as integers; NaN is exactly the case `|v| > 0x7F800000`. This is one instruction per operand and needs no new constants.

The int32 variant in `ckernel_sfpu_binary_max_min.h` already demonstrates the structural pattern for correcting `SFPSWAP` — `SFPSETCC` on both registers, a second conditional `SFPSWAP`, then `SFPENCC`. The float32 path needs the analogous guard, keyed on the NaN test above rather than on sign.

For `clamp` / `hardtanh`, one guard on the input value before the two swaps is sufficient, since the bounds are compile-time scalars.

Note the `SFPLOADMACRO` fast paths (`binary_max_min_init`, `calculate_unary_max_min`) will need the same treatment as the `DISABLE_SFPLOADMACRO` paths, or the two will diverge.

### Success criteria

- [ ] `ttnn.maximum` / `ttnn.minimum` propagate NaN for both `+NaN` and `-NaN`, matching `torch.maximum` / `torch.minimum`
- [ ] `ttnn.clamp` / `ttnn.hardtanh` return NaN for NaN input, matching `torch.clamp` / `torch.nn.functional.hardtanh`
- [ ] Both the `SFPLOADMACRO` and `DISABLE_SFPLOADMACRO` paths are fixed and agree
- [ ] `max`/`min`/`clamp`/`hardtanh` added to the existing `_SPECIAL_FP32_GRID` coverage in `test_binary_comp_fp32.py`, or an equivalent special-value grid
- [ ] Non-NaN behaviour unchanged (verified here on 200,100 pairs: 0 mismatches)
- [ ] Confirmed on Blackhole (logic-identical file — same fix applies)

### Why this matters

NaN propagation is the standard signal that a computation has gone wrong. Silently substituting a finite operand converts a detectable failure into corrupted data that flows downstream unnoticed — `clamp` is especially exposed, since it turns NaN into a *plausible-looking* bound value.

These are public ttnn ops with direct torch counterparts whose NaN behaviour is explicitly specified. The repository already treats NaN correctness as a requirement for comparison operators and has both the test grid and the detection idiom in place; `max`, `min`, `clamp` and `hardtanh` are order relations that are not yet covered by either, and both pieces needed to cover them already exist in-tree.

The argument that at least one of `maximum`/`minimum` must be wrong needs no hardware measurement — it follows from `SFPSWAP` being a permutation, which the repository's own source and comments establish.

Happy to open a PR with the kernel change and a pytest extending the existing special-value grid to `max`/`min`/`clamp`/`hardtanh`, if that would be useful.

items.title: ttnn.fmod / ttnn.remainder (unary scalar): inverted fix-up loop and an unreachable guard return wrong-signed, out-of-range remainders - the binary kernels already carry the correct fix
items.body:
# ttnn.fmod / ttnn.remainder (unary scalar): inverted fix-up loop and an unreachable guard return wrong-signed, out-of-range remainders — the binary kernels already carry the correct fix

The scalar (unary) `fmod` and `remainder` kernels still carry their original 2023 reduction. The
tensor-tensor (binary) kernels were rewritten in 2026 and were given two corrections that the scalar
kernels never received — including one whose source comment describes exactly the failure the scalar
kernel exhibits.

The result is that for the same inputs, `ttnn.fmod(x, 3.0)` and `ttnn.fmod(x, tensor_of_3.0)` disagree,
and it is the scalar path that is wrong. Both are the same public op; the overload decides which kernel
runs:

- `fmod(Tensor, ScalarVariant)` → `ttnn::unary_fmod` → `fmod_tile` → `calculate_fmod`
  (`ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h`, 2023) — [`binary_composite_op.cpp:525-533`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/binary/device/binary_composite_op.cpp#L525-L533)
- `fmod(Tensor, Tensor)` → `invoke_binary_ng` → `fmod_binary_tile` → `_sfpu_binary_fmod_`
  (`ckernel_sfpu_binary_fmod.h`, 2026) — [`binary_ng_utils.cpp:443-448`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/binary_ng/device/binary_ng_utils.cpp#L443-L448)

```
fmod(14.999999, 3)   scalar kernel: 9.5367432e-07     binary kernel: 2.9999990     torch: 2.9999990
fmod(13.999999, 7)   scalar kernel: 9.5367432e-07     binary kernel: 6.9999990     torch: 6.9999990
fmod(7916.9995, 7)   scalar kernel: 0.00048828125     binary kernel: 6.9995117     torch: 6.9995117
```

These are errors of ~100% of the divisor at `|x/y|` of 2 to 1131 — orders of magnitude inside any
validity range that has been proposed for these ops, and against an issue
([#33746](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/33746)) that states the expectation as
"<1 ULP bf16 and fp32 accuracy."

### Summary

`calculate_fmod()`
([`ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h),
byte-identical on Wormhole and Blackhole) computes a truncated quotient and then tries to fix it up:

```c
v_elseif(exp < 23) {
    quotient = sfpi::as<sfpi::vFloat>(
        shft((shft(sfpi::as<sfpi::vUInt>(v * recip_val), (exp - 23))), (0 - (exp - 23))));
}
...
v_if(quotient > v * recip_val) { quotient = quotient - 1; }   // line 47 — unreachable
v_endif;
v = v - quotient * s;

v = sfpi::copysgn(v, val);                                    // line 53 — sign applied too early
...
constexpr auto iter = 10;
for (int l = 0; l < iter; l++) {
    v_if(v >= s) { v = s - v; }                               // lines 58-62 — inverted
    v_endif;
}
```

Three defects:

**(a) The guard on line 47 is unreachable.** `quotient` is `v * recip_val` with its low mantissa bits
masked to zero, so `quotient <= v * recip_val` holds by construction and the condition is never true.
Emulated over 2.8M inputs it fired 0 times. It needs to compare against the *unrounded* `v / s`; the
working form is `quotient * s > v`.

**(b) So the quotient over-estimate it was meant to catch goes uncorrected.** `recip_val` is a rounded
`1/y` (`unary_op_utils.cpp` passes `std::bit_cast<uint32_t>(1.0f / param0)`) and the multiply rounds
again, so `v * recip_val` can land on an integer that `v / y` sits just below. `v - n*y` is then
negative, and `copysgn` on line 53 discards that sign — so a remainder that should be just under `y`
is returned as just above `0`.

For `fmod(14.999999, 3)`: `fl(1/3) = 0.33333334` (above `1/3`), `14.999999 × 0.33333334 = 4.99999983`,
which is within half a float32 ULP of `5.0` and rounds to exactly `5.0f`; truncation leaves `5`;
`14.999999 - 15 = -9.5367432e-07`; `copysgn` makes it `+9.5367432e-07`.

**(c) The fix-up loop reduces in the wrong direction.** `v = s - v` produces the correct magnitude with
the wrong sign; the correct reduction is `v = v - s`. The loop is also self-disabling — once it fires,
`v = y - v <= 0 < y`, so the remaining nine iterations are unconditional no-ops (emulated over 1.2M
inputs: iteration 1 fired 5404 times, iterations 2-10 fired 0 times). And because `copysgn` runs
*before* the loop, negative inputs never satisfy `v >= s` and get no fix-up at all.

**The binary kernels already do both of these correctly.**
[`ckernel_sfpu_binary_fmod.h`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_fmod.h)
(2026):

```c
    v_if(result_abs >= b_abs) {
        v_if(result >= sfpi::vFloat(0.0f)) { result = result - b_abs; }   // subtract, not b - result
        v_else                            { result = result + b_abs; }
        v_endif;
    }
    ...
    // This fixes cases where a/b ≈ 0.9999999 but rounds to 1 due to reciprocal error
    v_if(a >= sfpi::vFloat(0.0f)) {
        v_if(result < sfpi::vFloat(0.0f)) { result = result + b_abs; }
```

and `_sfpu_binary_remainder_` in `ckernel_sfpu_binary_remainder.h` carries the same correction under the
comment *"reciprocal imprecision can cause floor() to be greater than the true floor value."* That is a
verbatim description of defect (b) — already diagnosed and fixed on the binary path, never applied to
the scalar path.

### Measured

Method note first, because it matters for how much weight these numbers carry: these are float32
emulations of each kernel's exact instruction sequence. To check the emulation is faithful, I ran it
against the three real-hardware rows posted in
[#37023](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/37023). It reproduces all three **bit-exactly**:

| x | y | reported device output | emulation |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16240345088.0 | 0.003662109375 | -2047.99267578125 | -2047.99267578125 |
| 24293408768.0 | 0.0054931640625 | -2047.989013671875 | -2047.989013671875 |
| 25635586048.0 | 0.00579833984375 | -2047.98828125 | -2047.98828125 |

(Those rows are the *binary* kernel; the same emulation harness produces the scalar-kernel numbers below.)

**Scalar kernel wrong where the binary kernel is right**, all well inside range:

| x | y | \|x/y\| | scalar (2023) | binary (2026) | torch | scalar error |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 14.999999 | 3 | 2^2.3 | 9.5367432e-07 | 2.9999990 | 2.9999990 | 100% of y |
| 13.999999 | 7 | 2^1.0 | 9.5367432e-07 | 6.9999990 | 6.9999990 | 100% of y |
| 29.999998 | 3 | 2^3.3 | 1.9073486e-06 | 2.9999981 | 2.9999981 | 100% of y |
| 7916.9995 | 7 | 2^10.1 | 0.00048828125 | 6.9995117 | 6.9995117 | 100% of y |
| 29999.998 | 3 | 2^13.3 | 0.001953125 | 2.9980469 | 2.9980469 | 99.9% of y |
| 55642.996 | 7 | 2^13.0 | 0.00390625 | 6.9960938 | 6.9960938 | 99.9% of y |
| 2089359.9 | 7 | 2^18.2 | 0.125 | 6.875 | 6.875 | 96.4% of y |

**Wrong sign and `|r| > |y|`** — from defect (c), which has no counterpart in the binary kernel:

| x | y | scalar | torch | |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 39999988 | 3 | **-1** | 1 | sign inverted |
| -39999988 | 3 | **-4** | -1 | negative input gets no fix-up; `\|r\|` = 1.3× `\|y\|` |
| 399999968 | 3 | **-29** | 2 | `\|r\|` = 9.7× `\|y\|` |

**Same inputs through both kernels**, 20000 samples per decade × divisors {3, 7, 2.5, 10, 0.75, 1.5},
counting results that are not bit-exact against `torch.fmod`:

| \|x\| | scalar kernel | binary kernel |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1–1e3 | 0 / 240000 | 0 / 240000 |
| 1e3–1e5 | **104 / 240000** | 0 / 240000 |
| 1e5–1e6 | **1966 / 240000** | 0 / 240000 |
| 1e6–1e7 | 29384 / 240000 | 21662 / 240000 |

Below `|x/y| ≈ 2^20` the binary kernel is exact and the scalar kernel is not. Above that both degrade,
which is the regime #37023 already describes.

**Exhaustive**, all 8388608 float32 values in `[10, 20)`: the failing inputs are exactly those one ULP
below an exact multiple of `y`.

| y | scalar kernel failures | which | binary kernel failures |
|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 3 | 1 | 14.999999 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 13.999999 | 0 |
| 1.5 | 2 | 13.499999, 14.999999 | 0 |

**`-inf` for finite inputs.** When `|x| * fl(1/y)` overflows — `x = 1e30, y = 1e-30`, both ordinary
float32 values — `quotient` becomes `inf`, `v - inf*y = -inf`, and the fix-up loop turns `+inf` into
`y - inf = -inf`. A function whose range is `[0, |y|)` returns `-inf`. Separately, `y = inf` gives
`quotient * s = 0 * inf = NaN`, so `fmod(x, inf)` returns `NaN` instead of `x`.

**`remainder` is affected identically** — `ckernel_sfpu_remainder.h` lines 184-203 are the same
construct, character for character:

| call | scalar kernel | torch |
|---|---:|---:|
| `remainder(14.999999, 3)` | 9.5367432e-07 | 2.9999990 |
| `remainder(7916.9995, 7)` | 0.00048828125 | 6.9995117 |
| `remainder(39999988, 3)` | **-1** | 1 |
| `remainder(-39999988, 3)` | **-4** | 2 |

### Relationship to existing issues

- **[#37023](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/37023) (open)** documents the large-`|x/y|`
  regime and proposes restricting validation to `|x/y| < 2^23` (fp32) / `2^7` (bf16). Everything in the
  tables above except the last two rows of the "same inputs" table is **inside** that bound — the
  smallest failing case is `|x/y| = 2`. So the proposed range restriction does not cover these, and the
  scalar kernel fails inside its own declared-valid region.

  One note on that issue's premise, offered as a technical correction rather than a disagreement about
  scope: `fmod` never needs to represent `x/y`. C specifies the result as `x - ny` with the same sign as
  `x` and magnitude less than `|y|` (C11 7.12.10.1), and that value is always exactly representable in
  the input format — which is why `glibc` and `torch` return exact results at any ratio, by reducing with
  power-of-two-scaled subtractions rather than by forming `x/y`. It is achievable here too: the reference
  implementation below is bit-exact against `math.fmod` at a ratio of `2^199` given enough reduction
  rounds. The large-ratio failures follow from single-step reduction, not from float32.

- **[#33746](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/33746) (closed)** sets the accuracy target at
  "<1 ULP bf16 and fp32". The scalar kernel misses that by roughly `10^7` ULP at `|x/y| = 2`.

- **[#12835](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/12835)** ("Incorrect results with fmod and
  remainder from negative inputs", closed 2024) is the closest prior report. The `copysgn`-before-the-loop
  ordering that makes negative inputs skip the fix-up entirely is still present.

No open issue covers defects (a), (b), (c), or the `-inf` leak.

### Files

- `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h` (WH)
- `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/blackhole/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_fmod.h` (BH, byte-identical)
- `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_remainder.h` (WH, lines 184-203)
- `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/blackhole/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_remainder.h` (BH)

Fix templates already in-repo: `ckernel_sfpu_binary_fmod.h` and `ckernel_sfpu_binary_remainder.h`.

### Proposed fix

The minimal fix is to port the binary kernels' two corrections to the scalar kernels: replace the
unreachable `quotient > v * recip_val` with the working `quotient * s > v`, and replace the
`v = s - v` loop with the binary kernel's signed add/subtract correction applied *before* `copysgn`.
That alone restores the 1e3–1e6 rows above to 0 failures.

Going further and making the scalar path exact over a wide range is also possible, using the chunked
multiply already present in `compute_unsigned_remainder_small_b()` (11-bit chunks, chosen so each
partial product stays exact) lifted from the integer path onto the float path:

1. Split the divisor once: `y_hi` = `y` with its low 12 mantissa bits cleared, `y_lo = y - y_hi` (exact
   by Sterbenz). Each holds at most 12 significant bits.
2. Per round, scale the *divisor* by `2^k` via `setexp` (exact) so that `|r| / (y·2^k) < 2^12`. This
   bounds the quotient to 12 bits and makes `|r| * recip` structurally incapable of overflowing — which
   removes the `-inf` mode rather than patching around it.
3. `r = (r - q·y_hi) - q·y_lo`. With `q` at 12 bits and each chunk at 12 bits, both products are exact.
4. Carry the sign through the rounds; do not clamp mid-loop. An over-estimated `q` simply makes `r`
   negative and the next round shrinks `|r|`. Clamping is what converts an overshoot into a sign error.
5. Normalise with `r -= y` / `r += y`, never `y - r`.

Emulated, bit-exact against `math.fmod`, 300000 samples per decade:

| \|x\| | current scalar kernel | proposed |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1e2–1e4 | 26 / 300000 | **0 / 300000** |
| 1e4–1e6 | 2386 / 300000 | **0 / 300000** |
| 1e6–1e8 | 182150 / 300000 | **0 / 300000** |
| 1e8–1e10 | 226506 / 300000 | **0 / 300000** |

Three rounds cover `|x/y| < 2^36`; each further round buys 12 bits. Two limits are worth stating
plainly. Beyond the round count a residual remains (full fp32 range would need 22 rounds — a cost
decision, not a correctness one; `fmod(1e30, 1e-30)`, ratio `2^199`, is bit-exact at 22). And divisors
within about `2^12` of `FLT_MIN` break the split because `y_lo` falls subnormal; `y` is a compile-time
literal so the host can screen for it. Both are reliably detectable — `|r| >= |y|` after normalisation
is true for every out-of-coverage input tested and false for every in-coverage one — so the out-of-range
case can be clamped or given a documented validated range the way `i1` documents `[-10, 10]`, rather
than silently returning a wrong finite number.

Cost should be roughly neutral: the 10-iteration loop being removed can be shown to do at most one
useful iteration, freeing ~20 SFPU ops; three reduction rounds cost on the order of 30. That is an
instruction-count estimate, not a measurement.

### Success criteria

- [ ] `|fmod(x, y)| < |y|` and `sign(fmod(x, y)) == sign(x)` for all finite inputs
- [ ] scalar and binary paths agree — `ttnn.fmod(x, 3.0) == ttnn.fmod(x, full_like(x, 3.0))`
- [ ] bit-exact against `torch.fmod` / `torch.remainder` over the supported `|x/y|` range
- [ ] no `inf`/`NaN` output for finite `x` and finite non-zero `y`
- [ ] tests extended past `|x| <= 100`: the current sweeps (`test_backward_fmod.py`,
      `test_backward_remainder.py`) use `data_gen_with_range(..., -100, 100)` in bfloat16 with PCC
      comparison, which is why this was never caught
- [ ] add exact-multiple-neighbourhood cases (`nextafter(n*y, 0)`) — these are the sparse low-magnitude
      failures, and a PCC threshold over a tile cannot see a handful of wrong elements
- [ ] confirm on Blackhole (byte-identical files)

### Why this matters

`fmod` is exact for floats, so there is no accuracy tolerance to negotiate here, and `|r| < |y|` is a
hard invariant callers are entitled to rely on. The scalar and binary paths of the same public op
currently disagree on ordinary inputs, with the scalar path returning ~100% -of-divisor errors and,
at larger ratios, wrong signs and out-of-range magnitudes. The failures are silent, finite and
plausible-looking, and the periodic-wrapping uses these ops exist for — angle reduction, index
wrapping, positional encodings — land squarely in the affected regime.

---

*Method: numbers are float32 emulations of each kernel's exact instruction sequence (numpy `float32`;
`exexp` / `shft` / `copysgn` semantics read from `sfpi_lib.h`); I do not have a device. The emulation
reproduces the three device rows posted in #37023 bit-exactly, which is the basis for trusting it.
`recip_val` is modelled as `1.0f / param0` per `unary_op_utils.cpp`. Defects (a) and (c) are properties
of the source and hold independent of any numeric assumption. `math.fmod` in float64 is the reference
because floating-point `fmod` is exact.*

Implementation and tests are ready; happy to open a PR.

items.title: floor_div spends 5 of its 9 device kernels on a NaN/Inf guard that isfinite does in one pass
items.body:
### Summary

`ttnn.floor_div(tensor, tensor)` dispatches **9 device kernels** for what is arithmetically two divides and a select. Five of those nine exist only to detect non-finite values, and a single `ttnn::isfinite` replaces all five.

### Current implementation

`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/binary/device/binary_composite_op.cpp`:

```cpp
Tensor floor_div(const Tensor& input_a, const Tensor& input_b, const std::optional<MemoryConfig>& output_mem_config) {
    Tensor temp = ttnn::div(input_a, input_b, false, std::nullopt, std::nullopt, output_mem_config);
    Tensor result = ttnn::div(input_a, input_b, false, "floor", std::nullopt, output_mem_config);
    // floor(nan, inf, -inf) = nan, inf, -inf
    return ttnn::where(
        ttnn::logical_or(
            ttnn::eq(temp, std::nanf("")),
            ttnn::logical_or(
                ttnn::eq(temp, std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity()),
                ttnn::eq(temp, -std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity()))),
        temp,
        result);
}
```

The three `eq` plus two `logical_or` calls are five separate dispatches, each a full DRAM read + write of the tensor.

### Measured cost

Profiled on **p150b (Blackhole)**, bfloat16, summing `DEVICE KERNEL DURATION` over every kernel the op dispatches:

| shape | kernels | device time |
|---|---|---|
| `1x1x32x32` | 9 | 23698 ns |
| `1x1x512x1024` | 9 | 81475 ns |

Per-kernel breakdown at `1x1x32x32`: the two divides cost 2333 + 2228 + 1356 ns, the **guard costs 3901 + 3861 + 3887 + 2204 + 2141 = 15994 ns**, and the final select 1787 ns. The guard is roughly two thirds of the total.

### Proposed fix

`ttnn::isfinite` already exists as a single SFPU unary and covers NaN, +Inf and -Inf together:

```cpp
return ttnn::where(ttnn::isfinite(temp, output_mem_config), result, temp);
```

This takes the op from 9 dispatches to 5:

| shape | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1x1x32x32` | 23698 ns | 8995 ns | **-62.0%** |
| `1x1x512x1024` | 81475 ns | 45776 ns | **-43.8%** |

### Correctness

The rewrite is **bit-identical** to the existing expression. Verified by evaluating both formulations on-device over the same inputs, covering finite values, division by zero and `0/0`:

```
       num ['7', '-7', '5', '0', '6', '-6', '1', '0']
       den ['2', '2', '-2', '3', '0', '0', '0', '0']
       OLD ['3', '-4', '-3', '0', 'inf', '-inf', 'inf', 'inf']
       NEW ['3', '-4', '-3', '0', 'inf', '-inf', 'inf', 'inf']
OLD == NEW everywhere: True
```

Worth recording: the `ttnn::eq(temp, std::nanf(""))` term **can never be true**, because NaN compares unequal to everything under IEEE 754. So the NaN case was already falling through to the floored value rather than propagating `temp`. `isfinite` preserves that same observable behaviour, so this is not a behaviour change, but the dead comparison is why the guard never did what its comment claims for NaN.

### Separately observed (not addressed here)

`ttnn.div(0, 0)` returns `inf` on device where torch returns `nan` (visible in the last column above). That originates in `div` itself, predates this issue, and is not affected by the change proposed here.

### Test status

`tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_div_ops.py` — 116 passed, 8 skipped, 2 xfailed.

items.title: `sfpi::lut2`/`sfpi::lut2_sign` use the WH/BH LUT table registers on Quasar, giving silently wrong results
items.body:
## Summary
On Quasar, SFPLUTFP32 takes its piecewise table from the SFPU **constant** LRegs, not the general ones:

| | slopes | intercepts | looked-up value |
|---|---|---|---|
| WH/BH  | LReg0-2  | LReg4-6   | LReg3 |
| Quasar | LReg9-11 | LReg12-14 | LReg3 |

Segment selection, the input register and the mode encoding are all unchanged from WH/BH, only the table
source moved. This matches the SFPCONFIG `config_dest` naming in
`tt_metal/tt-llk/tt_llk_quasar/instructions/assembly.yaml:7521` ("LUT constant lreg[9]/lreg[10]",
"Programmable constant lreg[11..14]").

sfpi still emits the WH/BH mapping, with two consequences:

1. `lut2()` / `lut2_sign()` materialize the six table words into `LReg0-2`/`LReg4-6`, which the LUT never
   reads. A kernel ported from WH/BH, whose init loads the table into exactly those registers, compiles
   clean and returns wrong results.
2. There is no sfpi way to load the registers the LUT does read: `sfpconfig` rejects dests 9 and 10.

Note the instruction itself is fine: sfpi pins the looked-up value to LReg3 and the result to an
allocated LReg, both correct here. Preloading LRegs 9-14 with `ckernel::math::_sfpu_load_config32_` and
then calling `lut2_sign()` passes on emu-quasar for every format and Dest width (approximate-GELU sweep).
So what needs fixing is the table setup, not instruction selection.

## Environment
- `GCC: (tenstorrent/sfpi:7.67.0[761]) 15.1.0`, target `tt-qsr32-tensix`
- Affects `__builtin_rvtt_sfplutfp32_3r` / `__builtin_rvtt_sfplutfp32_6r` (part 1) and
  `__builtin_rvtt_sfpwriteconfig_v` (part 2)
- WH/BH unaffected, their LUT really does read LReg0-2/LReg4-6

## Part 1: table operands land in LReg0-2/4-6

```cpp
#include <cstdint>
namespace ckernel { volatile uint32_t *instrn_buffer; }  // sfpi headers' only external dep
#include "sfpi.h"
using namespace sfpi;

void gelu_appx() {  // Blackhole's calculate_gelu_appx, verbatim
    vUInt l0 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg0], l1 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg1], l2 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg2];
    vUInt l4 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg4], l5 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg5], l6 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg6];
    vFloat in = dst_reg[0];
    dst_reg[0] = in * vConstFloatPrgm0 + lut2_sign(in, l0, l1, l2, l4, l5, l6);
}
```
```
riscv-tt-elf-g++ -mcpu=tt-qsr32-tensix -O2 -std=c++17 -c -I <sfpi>/include repro.cpp
riscv-tt-elf-objdump -d repro.o
```

### Observed
```asm
sfpload     L3,0,0,7,0,0
sfplutfp32  L0,2
sfpmad      L3,L3,L12,L0,0
sfpstore    L3,0,0,7,0,0
```
No SFPCONFIG, so the six operands are meant to be the table. With the table loaded into LReg0-2/4-6 (what
Blackhole's `gelu_init` does) this miscompares on emu-quasar for every format and Dest width. With the
same table in LRegs 9-14 it is correct.

Two more consequences once the table *is* in the right place:
- the six operands still tie up LReg0-2/4-6 for nothing, leaving two general LRegs. Our approximate-GELU
  loop lost its fused multiply-add over this: 5 ops (`SFPMULI` + `SFPADD`) against 4 (`SFPMAD`)
  hand-written, since nothing is left to hold the 0.5.
- `vConstFloatPrgm0` cannot hold a kernel constant the way it does on Blackhole. On Quasar that is
  LReg12, one of the intercept words.

### Expected
`lut2*` should read the table from the constant LRegs on Quasar (needs part 2), ideally without requiring
six dead operands.

## Part 2: `sfpconfig` rejects dests 9 and 10

```cpp
void load_lut_table() {
    constexpr impl_::LRegFile::vCReg<vUInt> lut9(9), lut10(10), lut11(11);
    lut11 = vUInt(0x38003852u);   // ok, emits sfploadi + sfpconfig 11
    lut9  = vUInt(0x37E7322Bu);   // rejected
    lut10 = vUInt(0x38E138F3u);   // rejected
}
```

### Observed
```
Error: unsupported value `9' for mod operand (permitted mask is 0xf9ff
Error: illegal operands `sfpconfig 9,0,0'
Error: unsupported value `10' for mod operand (permitted mask is 0xf9ff
Error: illegal operands `sfpconfig 10,0,0'
```
`0xf9ff` clears exactly bits 9 and 10, the two LUT-constant destinations. Dests 11-14 assemble fine. This
is the real blocker: without it a LUT table cannot be loaded from sfpi at all.

### Expected
Accept `config_dest` 9 and 10 on Quasar (the ISA defines them, the hardware implements them), or expose
some other way to load the LUT table. I assume the restriction is there to protect `vConst0`/`vConst1`
(0.0/1.0); on Quasar those registers are dual-purpose, so on this target it blocks a legitimate use.

## Workaround in use
`ckernel_sfpu_gelu.h` loads the table through the LLK config helper and keeps the loop in sfpi with six
dummy operands:

```cpp
// gelu_init, not expressible in sfpi (part 2)
ckernel::math::_sfpu_load_config32_(0x9, 0x37E7, 0x322B);   // six pairs, LRegs 9-14

// loop, plain sfpi. The six operands only exist to satisfy the intrinsic.
vUInt l0 = l_reg[LRegs::LReg0]; /* ... l1, l2, l4, l5, l6 ... */
vFloat in = dst_reg[0];
dst_reg[0] = in * 0.5f + lut2_sign(in, l0, l1, l2, l4, l5, l6);   // immediate, not vConstFloatPrgm0
```

## Impact
- Silent wrong answers for anyone porting a LUT-based activation from WH/BH to Quasar.
- LUT kernels cannot express their table load in sfpi, so they keep an arch-specific init.
- Six general LRegs are spent on operands the hardware ignores, which costs instructions.
